title: Man who died was off meds; Coroner cites excited delirium as cause of death Discounts role of pepper-spraying by police officers: [ONT Edition]
article: Fifty-eight per cent of the deaths from excited delirium occur in patients with psychiatric illness who have come off their medication, Ontario's deputy coroner told an inquest yesterday as he gave the five-person jury a beginner's course in the condition, which can cause a sudden and unexpected death.

Psychiatric illness is the most common underlying condition in cases of excited delirium, said Jim Cairns, as he tried to put the phenomenon into context so the inquest could establish the role it might have played in the death of 24-year-old Nicholas Blentzas on June 22, 2002.
Blentzas, who had a history of mental illness, and according to his family was acting strangely and had gone off his medication, died suddenly that night.
Police were called to his apartment building after neighbours complained that he was trying to break into his apartment with a fire extinguisher.
According to witnesses there was a struggle with police, who used pepper spray to try to restrain him.
They eventually subdued and handcuffed him, and then he suddenly died. By the time paramedics and the ambulance arrived, his heart had stopped.
The police were cleared of any wrongdoing in the case by the province's Special Investigations Unit, but an inquest was called because the death occurred in police custody.

In his opening statement, David Carruthers, counsel for the coroner, told the jury that when the police arrived that night Blentzas told the officers he had "two billion worth of equipment in the apartment."
He also told them that his mother and brother were in England and lived in a castle and he had lost his keys.

As Carruthers recapped events, Blentzas' sister cried in the courtroom. He told jury members that evidence would be presented that Blentzas died as a result of excited delirium, which also occurs in drug users or alcoholics who go off drugs or alcohol.

There are 13 signs and symptoms of excited delirium, including bizarre or aggressive behaviour, impaired thinking, acute paranoia, panic, apparent ineffectiveness of pepper spray, unexpected physical strength and sudden tranquillity, said Cairns, an expert on the condition.
Excited delirium causes a surge in adrenal hormones that increases heart rate, blood pressure and respiratory rate, he said.
That makes those who are suffering from excited delirium "susceptible to cardiac arrhythmias" and they die, the deputy coroner said.
It is also very hard to treat because it all happens within five to 10 minutes.
The best course of action is to sedate the person and get him to the hospital as soon as possible. But even there it can be fatal.

What's more, Cairns testified, there are certain restraint positions - such as being held face down with hands cuffed behind your back - that increase the risk of death in these individuals, or as Cairns said, "tip the balance."
But he also acknowledged that these positions often have to be used to restrain someone.
In his testimony, Cairns discounted the role of pepper spray in the deaths associated with excited delirium.
There has been no evidence in Ontario that links the use of pepper spray to death in these kinds of cases, he said.
